text.en: You drink water, breathe air and eat food that grew in soil. All came from nature. These gifts are called natural resources, and we must use them wisely.

A natural resource is something from nature that we use, such as air, water, soil, sunlight, forests, minerals and fossil fuels. Sunlight and wind are naturally renewed. Fresh water is renewed by the water cycle, but a local supply can fall if water is used faster than it arrives. Non-renewable resources are limited and take millions of years to form, such as coal, petroleum and natural gas.
Air gives oxygen for breathing and moves as wind. Water is needed for drinking, farming and industry. Only a small part of Earth's water is fresh and easy to use. The Sun gives light and heat, and we can use solar energy for heating and electricity.
Forests provide wood, foods, medicines and habitats. Leaves can trap some dust, and roots and leaf litter help slow the loss of soil.
As rocks weather, their fragments mix with decayed remains and other material to form soil. A soil profile may show topsoil, subsoil and underlying rock. Topsoil is rich in humus and supports plants. Rocks contain minerals. Iron can be obtained from iron ore. Coal is mined too, but it is a fossil fuel.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from remains of plants and animals buried millions of years ago. Burning them gives energy but causes pollution.
Reduce, reuse and recycle. Save water, switch off lights, plant trees and use public transport.

Imagine a town on our map with a stream, a tree-covered hill and a sunny field. Each can supply something useful. Trace the connection from a feature to something people or other living things need.
A flag hangs down in still air and stretches when a breeze arrives. Air is present at both times. The flag gives us evidence that the air is moving when it stretches.
Air is a mixture of gases. Oxygen is one of them, and animals use it in respiration. Air around us also contains nitrogen and smaller amounts of other gases.
Picture cool shade next to a warm patch of sunlight. Sunlight warms surfaces, and a solar panel can turn some of the energy it receives into electricity.
A wind turbine has blades that turn when wind pushes them. The machine uses that movement to generate electricity. Its output depends on the wind at the site.
Follow rain on the map. Some flows downhill into streams, and some soaks into spaces in soil and rock. Water below the ground is called groundwater, and wells can draw on it.

board.text: Rain → surface flow or soaking in

text.en: Imagine a village well after a dry season. If people use more groundwater than enters the ground, the water level can fall. Saving water and giving rain a place to soak in can help the supply.

board.text: Compare groundwater used with water added
Allow rain to soak into the ground

text.en: Look at a forest from the canopy down to the ground. Birds may nest in branches, insects may use bark, and fungi can break down fallen leaves. A forest offers many different places to live.

board.text: Branches, bark and leaf litter are habitats

text.en: After heavy rain, compare a leaf-covered slope with a bare one. Leaves soften the impact of raindrops, and roots hold some soil in place. Both can reduce the amount carried away by water.

board.text: Roots help hold soil in place

text.en: Look at a sketch of soil with dark material near the surface and more rock fragments deeper down. Humus is decayed plant and animal material. Topsoil often contains more humus and supports many roots.

board.text: Lower layers: changes in the amount of rock

text.en: Weathering can break a rock into smaller pieces that stay where the rock was. Erosion happens when water or wind carries soil and rock pieces away. Look for movement to tell the processes apart.
Compare a piece of granite with a steel paper clip. Granite is a rock made of minerals. Much of the iron used to make steel comes from rocks mined as iron ore.

board.text: Granite is a rock containing minerals

text.en: Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from the remains of ancient life under different conditions. Burning them releases energy and adds carbon dioxide to the air. They take far longer to form than we take to use them.

Classify a forest, sunlight and a coal deposit. A forest can regrow when protected, sunlight keeps arriving, and coal takes much longer to form than a human lifetime. This helps explain how their supplies differ.

board.text: Coal: forms over very long times

text.en: Think of a workbook with unused backs on its pages. Use a back for notes before adding the sheet to paper recycling. Using the sheet again saves a new one and recycling can recover the material later.

A school has a dripping tap, a bare playground slope and lights in empty rooms. Match a practical response to each: report the leak, cover exposed soil with plants where suitable, and switch off lights when rooms are empty.

Pick one of those changes and decide what you could observe before and after. You might compare the amount of water collected from a dripping tap during the same length of time before and after a repair.

board.text: Compare the same measurement before and after

text.en: It is a fossil fuel and takes millions of years to form.
Once used up it cannot be replaced soon.

prompt.en: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources.

points.en: Renewable and non-renewable resources differ in how fast they are replaced.
Forests, soil and water are precious.
